film.caption: The Italian Flag, 2:57. Tesa 41, October 2026
film.credit: Sound on; captions in the player menu
p1: This autumn the Armenian Pavilion made a flag. Not Armenia’s red, blue and apricot, but Italy’s green, white and red: painted by hand in Tesa 41, built from the same kind of units the studio works with all year, and stood up on its own feet.
p2: It raises an obvious question, and we asked it ourselves, on camera: is it a little strange that we’re making an Italian flag from the Armenian Pavilion? This post doesn’t settle that question. It lays out what we have found while living with it.
fig.painting-green: Zadik Zadikian painting the green of the Italian flag
p3: In 1954 Jasper Johns painted a flag. He later explained that his early subjects, flags, targets, numbers and maps, were “things the mind already knows”, and that using them “gives me room to work on other levels.” A flag is the purest case. Nobody has to design it, and everyone recognises it before they have really looked. That frees the artist to make the looking itself the subject.
p4: Johns kept returning to it: a white flag, a flag on an orange field, three flags stacked so that each steps toward you. The Metropolitan Museum puts the open question well. The flag may signify flatness; it may connote America, or the politics of the moment in which you stand before it; “or the flag may connote none of these things.”
p5: The studio’s flag comes from the same place and goes somewhere else. Johns made a painting that is also a flag. Here the flag is made of things: blocks of colour, the size of the body, which can be lifted, carried, taken apart and set up again. What Johns did with the eye, the studio does with weight.
p6: The studio has answered Johns more directly too. Jasper Johns’ American Flag is a study for three free-standing slabs, blue, white and red, with a star cut through all three, so that from one spot the stars line up. There are no stripes and no canton: just the three colours, stood up as sculpture, and a hole the shape of a star.
fig.af-study: Jasper Johns’ American Flag, 2026. Study for three free-standing slabs with a star cut through all three. Rendering
p7: Walk around it and the flag comes and goes. Head on, the star is a window through blue to white to red. From the side there is no flag at all, only three slabs standing apart.
p8: The tricolour was first adopted as a flag by an Italian state, the Cispadane Republic, at Reggio Emilia on 7 January 1797. It was a new kind of sign: a people’s flag rather than a dynasty’s. And it is striking how little the state says about what it means. Italy gives its three colours no official meaning; the meanings have been supplied by poets, by families, by football crowds, by whoever happens to be holding it.
p9: That openness is part of what makes it workable as material. A flag is, in one description, “only a piece of cloth”, and yet people love it, mourn under it and cross the world for it. Zadik put it more simply, standing in front of the finished piece: “There are three colours, but loaded with message.”
fig.assembling: Zadik Zadikian and an assistant assembling the Italian flag
h2.song: A song about a sewn flag
p10: There is an older thread between the two countries, and it runs through a flag. Armenia’s national anthem began as a poem by Mikayel Nalbandian, written in 1859: the song of an Italian girl who sews a tricolour for her brother as he goes to fight for Italy. The anthem’s opening words are hers.
p11: She is a character in a poem, not a historical person, and Armenia chose its own flag in 1918 for its own reasons. We don’t want to make more of the link than it can carry. But it is hard not to notice: for more than a century Armenians have sung an Italian girl’s words about making a flag by hand, and now an Armenian studio in Venice is making her flag by hand.
p12: The studio has not left its own flag out. Armenian Flag Stack lays red, blue and apricot units in rings, each ring leaving a gap on every face, so that the stripes spiral upward in colour and in space. Armenia’s flag law gives its colours meanings that Italy’s never fixed: red for the Armenian Highland and the struggle to survive, blue for the will to live beneath peaceful skies, apricot for the creative, hard-working nature of the people.
fig.stack: Armenian Flag Stack, 2026. Pigmented plaster units. Rendering of the proposed work in Republic Square, Yerevan
p13: Venice is the right place to notice it. The first book ever printed in Armenian was made here, in 1511 or 1512. Since 1717 the Mekhitarist monks of San Lazzaro have kept an Armenian monastery and library in the lagoon, and for two centuries they printed books there. Armenians have been guests in this city for a very long time, and it has been a generous host. If the flag is anything, it may be a greeting returned: between neighbours, or siblings, not a debt being paid.
h2.feet: A flag on its own feet
p14: Asked how he came to make it, Zadik didn’t reach for history at all. “It came to me very naturally,” he said. “It’s an extension of what I’m doing. You tune into simplicity, blocks of colour, and then it’s natural: where do you start from? You start from your roots, you start from your environment.” For a studio working inside the Arsenale, at the edge of a lagoon, under an Italian sky, the environment is Italy.
p15: And then there are the feet. “I wanted to put feet underneath, so that the piece will stand. The flag should have its own feet.” A flag usually needs a pole, a wall or a hand. This one stands up by itself, and because it is built from units it can also come apart. Push a block and the structure has already changed. Two people can carry a section. It is a national sign that is also, quite literally, a set of building blocks.
fig.in-front: Zadik Zadikian in front of the Italian flag in the studio
p16: The studio has been thinking at other scales too. Italian Flags is a proposal for three folded slabs of pigmented cement, standing on a hillside near Gubbio, in Umbria: not raised on a pole but set into the land like a building. It exists so far as drawings and renderings; the images below are renderings, not photographs.
p17: So: why the Italian flag, from the Armenian Pavilion? We have several answers, and we hold all of them loosely.
p18: Because a flag is something the mind already knows, and that leaves room to work on other levels. Because Italy’s colours come without an official meaning, and can take the weight of a new one. Because an Armenian poem once imagined an Italian girl sewing this flag. Because Venice has been host to Armenians for five centuries. Because you start from your roots and your environment, and the studio’s environment, this year, is Italy.
p19: Or, as someone said in the studio one afternoon in September, remembering one of Johns’s flag paintings: “Is that a flag? Is that a flag?”
p20: The Italian flag is in the studio at Tesa 41. Come and see it, and tell us what you think it is.
